Prioritise a feature backlog by picking pairs

Scoring twenty features 1 to 10 gives you twenty 8s. Asking "which would you build first?" between two at a time makes people trade off, and the order falls out of the answers.

Why picking pairs works here

  • Each person answers alone on their own phone, so the loudest voice in the meeting doesn't set the order.
  • The combined result shows the team's order, how much people agree (a 0 to 1 score), and each feature's best-to-worst place across people. A feature one person ranks 1st and another 11th is the one to talk about before you commit.
  • Every place comes with a range ("rank 3, plausibly 2 to 5"), so you can see which positions the answers actually settle and which are close.

What it doesn't do: It ranks what your team prefers, not what customers will pay for. Put customer evidence in the list ("Requested by 14 accounts: CSV export") if you want it weighed.

Compared with what you'd use today

RICE or ICE scoring, dot voting, MoSCoW, or a paid pairwise tool. Scoring frameworks need numbers nobody has; dot voting rewards whoever votes last. This is free and keeps each person's picks private until they share a code.

Under the hood: a Bradley-Terry model refit after every answer, an adaptive question picker, and a stop rule checked against simulated respondents, including ones whose picks are close calls. The method and its measurements.
